channel.title: Sextant
channel.description: Updates for Sextant, a business's data warehouse native on the Mac.

item.title: Version 0.1.3
item.description:
The warehouse is a copy, and this release is mostly about saying whether it is still the same as what it was copied from.

New:

  • Count a table against its source. Sources now has a Check beside each table: it asks the source for its rows month by month, holds them against the copy here, and names the months that disagree — a month an incremental sync skipped, a month that still holds rows the source has deleted, a sync that failed half way. It reads the source and writes nothing.
  • Total a number column beside the rows. A month can hold the right number of rows and the wrong amounts in them, which no count of rows will ever see. The total is kept exact to the last cent, on both sides.
  • Read again the months a check found wrong. The copy's rows for those months are taken out and the source's are read in their place, and the table is counted once more to show that it agrees. It is the only way a row deleted at the source ever leaves the copy, and it reads only the months named rather than the whole table.
  • Light, dark, or whatever the Mac is doing, in Settings.
  • A filter box on Sources, for a project with more tables than a screenful.
  • A new project asks for a name and an icon, and its Overview then asks for one thing at a time rather than offering four at once.

Taken out, until somebody asks for them back:

  • Alerts in Slack.
  • Publishing tables to PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery, Google Sheets or files. The Destination screen is now the Warehouse screen. A first release is better at saying what the numbers are than at copying them elsewhere.
  • A project that had either of them opens and runs as it did, but what it had set up for them is forgotten the next time the project is saved.

Fixed:

  • Closing a project comes back to the projects window rather than leaving nothing on screen.
  • Stopping a sync, a build or a read of the warehouse is no longer reported as a fault.
  • The Cancel button in Add a Source was cut in half, a conversation in Ask could overlap the one below it, and the Recommend sheet's rows are laid out properly.
  • The filter field on Sources said nothing at all to a screen reader.

Requires macOS 26. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.

item.title: Version 0.1.2
item.description:
This release is about how Sextant looks, and how it reads out loud.

On a wide display a paragraph used to run to 140 characters and a row's name sat a long way from its figure. Every screen now holds its content to a width you can read across and shares one spacing scale, so the app looks like one thing rather than eleven.

Some of that was not polish but bugs:

  • Explore's SQL editor took the whole window on a tall screen. It has a ceiling now, so you see about twice as many rows of your result.
  • The Get started checklist's buttons sat at the far edge of the card, a long way from the step they belong to.
  • A paused briefing looked exactly like a running one.
  • The starter tiles on Models and Briefings began their text at three different heights.

VoiceOver could not name a single control in Sextant before this release: every icon-only button and every switch announced nothing at all. All of them are named now, across thirty screens, sheets and settings panes, each one checked against the accessibility tree a screen reader actually reads, and the SQL editor says what it is when you land in it. Where the app animates, reduced motion is honoured.

One fix underneath the surface: half of all timestamps written into a project's file were a millisecond early, so a project saved twice never compared cleanly against itself. Nothing misbehaved, but no one could diff a project file. They are written correctly from now on.

Requires macOS 26.

item.title: Version 0.1.1
item.description:
This release exists to prove that updating works.

0.1.0 shipped with Sparkle wired in and an update feed nobody had ever updated from. Nothing about the app has changed since: this is the same build at a new version number, published so that a copy of 0.1.0 can find it, verify its signature and install it — and so that the next release that does carry changes is not the first one to try.

If your copy offered you this update and you are reading these notes inside it, the thing it was meant to prove is proved.

item.title: Version 0.1.0
item.description:
The first release.

Sextant keeps a business's data on its own Mac. It syncs from the databases, files and services you already have into a local DuckDB warehouse, models that data with SQL you own, and answers questions about it in plain words — every figure shown with the query behind it. Nothing leaves the machine unless you publish it somewhere yourself.

What it does:

  • Syncs from PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, MongoDB, BigQuery, Google Sheets, CSV, Parquet, JSON and Excel files, and object storage (S3, R2, GCS, MinIO), Delta Lake and Iceberg included — through an SSH tunnel where the server sits behind a bastion.
  • Copies a large table a range of its key at a time, so a cancel, a failure or a quit resumes rather than starts again.
  • Models the data with dbt-shaped SQL files you own, built as a graph with tests that gate whatever reads them. Claude proposes the staging, core and mart models for what you have synced.
  • Keeps a field guide: what each table and column means, what one row is, which rows every answer should leave out, and what a coded column's values stand for. The warehouse works out much of it by itself, and Sextant can read the codebase that wrote the data for the rest, checking every meaning against your own rows before offering it.
  • Writes those meanings into SQL, so a status reads "done" everywhere downstream rather than 4.
  • Answers questions in plain words, with the queries and charts behind them, and tells you when a figure in an answer was worked out rather than queried.
  • Lets you write SQL yourself in Explore, with Claude's help when you want it.
  • Pins what matters to a dashboard, and says when a figure is unlike its own history.
  • Runs questions on a schedule as briefings, and exports any answer as a PDF.
  • Says something in Slack when an answer is wrong: no orders since this morning, a store under its floor, a load that never landed. It speaks when something changes and stays quiet while it stays changed.
  • Keeps every project fresh on its own schedule with no window open, from the menu bar.
  • Publishes what you build to PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery, Google Sheets or files, keeps the warehouse itself as a DuckLake in your own bucket if you want it there, and lets Claude Code and other assistants read it read-only over MCP.

Requires macOS 26. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.

Sextant is a codename and the app is early: expect rough edges, and please report what you find.
